title: Declaring a value that must never change
question: A program needs the number of days in a week and must never change it while running. Which kind of declaration expresses that intent best?
options: A constant: a named value bound once that cannot be reassigned afterwards
A variable that the code simply never assigns again, with nothing preventing a later change by mistake
A parameter: a named value that the caller supplies anew every time the code is executed
A literal: a fixed value typed directly into the code and repeated at every place where it is needed
explanation: A constant gives the value a name and lets the language reject any later assignment, so the intent is enforced and not just hoped for. A variable that is merely left alone offers no such protection. A parameter is chosen by the caller on each call, and repeating a literal everywhere hides its meaning and makes changes error-prone.

title: Adding text and a number
question: A variable holds the text "42" and the program must add 8 to it to obtain the number 50. What is needed first?
options: Renaming the variable that holds the text so that its name suggests that it contains a number
An explicit conversion (cast) of the text into a number, because text and numbers are different types
Declaring the number 8 again as text, so that the sum of both values becomes 50 automatically
Nothing at all, since the digits inside any text are always treated as a number by every operator
explanation: Text and numbers are different types, so the characters "42" must be converted into the number 42 before arithmetic makes sense. A variable name carries no meaning for the computer. Turning 8 into text would lead to joining characters ("428") instead of adding, and not every language converts text to numbers implicitly.

title: The remainder operator
question: What does `17 mod 5` (the remainder of an integer division) evaluate to?
explanation: Dividing 17 by 5 gives a quotient of 3 and leaves 17 - 3 * 5 = 2 as the remainder, which is what the remainder operator returns. The value 3 is the quotient, 3.4 would come from a division that keeps fractions, and 12 is not related to either result.

title: Reading a variable never assigned
question: A variable `total` is declared but no value is ever assigned to it. What is the risk of reading it?
options: It always holds zero, so reading it is safe in every language and the sum will be correct
It keeps the value of the most recently declared variable of the same type elsewhere in the program
The program pauses and asks the user to type a value the first time that the variable is needed
Its content is undefined or arbitrary, so the result may be an error, a default or leftover garbage
explanation: A declared variable without an assignment has no value chosen by the programmer. Depending on the language it may be rejected, hold a default, or contain whatever was left in that memory, so relying on it leads to bugs. It is not guaranteed to be zero, it does not borrow another variable's value, and programs never prompt the user on their own.

title: Counting loop iterations
question: How many times does the body of `for i from 1 to 5 do ... end` run, when both bounds are included?
options: 5 times, with i taking the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5
4 times, because the loop stops before the last bound value of 5 is ever used
6 times, because the counter is counted once more when the loop finishes and exits
5 times, with i taking the values 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 as counting always starts at zero
explanation: With both bounds included, the counter takes every value from 1 through 5, so the body runs five times. Stopping before 5 would run it four times, the extra exit check does not execute the body a sixth time, and the counter starts at the stated lower bound of 1 and not at zero.

title: A while loop that never changes its condition
question: Consider `x = 0` followed by `while x < 10 do print(x) end`. What happens when this runs?
options: It prints the values 0 to 9 and stops, because the loop adds one to x on every pass
It never ends, because nothing in the loop changes x and the condition stays true forever
It prints 0 once and stops, because a loop body is only allowed to run a single time
It prints nothing, because the condition is checked after the body has finished its work
explanation: A while loop repeats as long as its condition is true, and only the code written inside it can change that. Since x never changes from 0, the condition x < 10 is always true and the loop never terminates. Loops do not increment counters by themselves, they may run many times, and the condition is checked before the body.

title: Boundary value in a condition
question: Given `score = 50`, what does `if score >= 50 then print("pass") else print("fail") end` print?
options: fail, because 50 is not strictly greater than the limit of 50 used in the comparison
Both words, because the value is exactly on the limit and the two branches run together
pass, because the comparison is true when the score is equal to the limit
Nothing, because a comparison with equal values is neither true nor false for the program
explanation: The operator >= is true when the left value is greater than or equal to the right one, and 50 is equal to 50, so the first branch runs and prints pass. Only one branch of an if/else ever runs, a strict > would have printed fail, and a comparison always produces true or false.

title: Parameters and arguments
question: In `function area(width, height)` called as `area(3, 4)`, what are the values 3 and 4?
options: Parameters: the names declared in the function header that will receive values later
Return values: the results that the function hands back to the code that called it
Local variables: names created inside the body of the function while it is running
Arguments: the actual values passed in this call, received by the parameters width and height
explanation: Parameters are the names in the definition, while arguments are the concrete values supplied at a call, here 3 and 4. Return values go the other way, from the function to the caller, and local variables are created in the body and are not supplied by the caller.

title: Order of the arguments in a call
question: The function `subtract(a, b)` returns `a - b`. What does `subtract(3, 10)` return?
options: -7, because arguments are matched to parameters by position, so a is 3 and b is 10
7, because subtraction always reports the positive distance between the two arguments
7, because the function sorts the arguments from the largest to the smallest before using them
An error, because the first argument must always be larger than the second one in a subtraction
explanation: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, so a receives 3 and b receives 10, and 3 - 10 is -7. Functions do not reorder their arguments or take absolute values unless their code says so, and subtracting a larger number from a smaller one is perfectly valid.

title: Why extract repeated code into a function
question: A program repeats the same six lines of tax calculation in five different places. What is the main benefit of moving them into one function?
options: The calculation runs faster in every case, because a function call is always cheaper than inline code
The rule lives in a single definition, so fixing or changing it once updates every place that calls it
The six lines no longer need to be correct, since the computer checks functions separately on its own
The program stops using memory for those lines, because functions are kept only on disk until needed
explanation: A function gives the repeated logic one definition, so a bug fix or rule change is made once instead of in five copies that can drift apart. A call is not automatically faster, a function still has to be correct and tested, and its code occupies memory like any other code.

title: The first step in solving a problem
question: Before writing any code for a new problem, what should be done first?
options: Pick the data structure used on the previous project and adapt the problem so that it fits
Write the most optimised version straight away, because early design effort always pays off later
Restate the problem, confirm inputs, outputs and constraints, and work through a small example
Start coding the first idea that comes to mind and fix whatever fails whenever a test breaks
explanation: Understanding the problem comes first: restating it, checking inputs, outputs and limits, and solving a tiny example by hand exposes misunderstandings cheaply. Forcing a familiar structure, optimising before anything works and coding the first idea all risk solving the wrong problem.

title: Breaking a problem into subproblems
question: What does decomposing a problem into subproblems mean in practice?
options: Removing the hardest requirements so that the remaining problem is small enough to solve
Solving everything in one long block of steps so that no part can get out of sync with another
Giving each part of the problem to a different computer so that all of them run in parallel
Splitting it into smaller, simpler pieces that are solved and tested separately, then combined
explanation: Decomposition splits a big problem into smaller ones that are easier to understand, solve and test on their own, and then combines the partial results. Dropping requirements changes the problem, one giant block is harder to get right, and parallel machines are a separate execution choice and not what decomposition means.

title: An edge case for finding the largest value
question: A function must return the largest value in a list. Which input is an important edge case to decide on before coding?
options: An empty list, where no largest value exists and the behaviour must be defined
A list of ten values in random order, which is the kind of input used in every example
A list whose first value is the largest, since that is the only case needing a comparison
A list of positive whole numbers, since that is the most common kind of input in practice
explanation: Edge cases are inputs at the limits of what the function accepts, and an empty list has no largest value, so the design must choose between an error, a special result or forbidding it. The other inputs are ordinary cases that a first implementation already handles.

title: Tracing an algorithm by hand
question: What is a trace (also called a dry run) of an algorithm?
options: Running the finished program on the largest available input to measure how long it takes
Stepping through the algorithm by hand with a small input while recording how the variables change
Deleting the unused lines of the algorithm so that only the essential steps remain in place
Translating the algorithm from pseudocode into a different notation without ever executing it
explanation: A trace follows each step with a small concrete input and writes down the value of every variable as it changes, which reveals logic errors before or without running code. Timing a large run is benchmarking, deleting lines is cleanup, and changing notation does not check behaviour.

title: What a brute-force approach is
question: What defines a brute-force approach to a problem?
options: It always takes the locally best choice at each step and never reconsiders it later
It halves the input repeatedly and discards the half that cannot contain the answer
It tries every candidate solution and checks each one: simple and correct, but often slow
It stores the results of subproblems so that each of them is computed only one time
explanation: Brute force enumerates all candidates and tests them, so it is easy to get right but its cost grows quickly with the input. Always taking the best local choice is a greedy strategy, halving the input is how binary search works, and caching subproblem results is dynamic programming.

title: Which task takes constant time
question: Which task takes constant time, O(1), no matter how large the list of n items is?
options: Counting how many of the elements are equal to a given value
Printing every element of the list in order, one per line
Adding up all the numbers that are stored in the list
Reading the element at a known index of an array
explanation: Reading by index jumps straight to the position, so its cost does not depend on n. Counting matches, printing every element and summing all values each have to visit every item, so their cost grows linearly, O(n).

title: Dropping constants in Big O
question: An algorithm performs exactly 3n + 10 steps for n items. What is its Big O class?
options: O(n), because constant factors and lower-order terms are dropped
O(3n + 10), because Big O has to keep the exact number of steps performed
O(10), because the added constant is the part that dominates for large n
O(3n), because the multiplier is kept and only the added constant is ignored
explanation: Big O describes growth as n becomes large, so constant multipliers and smaller added terms are discarded, leaving O(n). Keeping the exact count or the multiplier 3 describes a particular machine and not the growth rate, and the constant 10 is the part that matters least for large n.

title: Worst case of a linear search
question: In the worst case, how many comparisons does a linear search make on a list of n items?
options: Only one, because the search stops as soon as it looks at the first element of the list
n, which happens when the target is the last element or is not in the list at all
About log n, because every comparison rules out half of the elements still under consideration
Exactly n / 2 every time, because the target is assumed to sit in the middle of the list
explanation: A linear search checks elements one by one, and in the worst case the target is last or absent, so all n elements are compared. One comparison is the best case, halving the candidates is binary search and needs sorted data, and the target position is not assumed.

title: What space complexity measures
question: What does the space complexity of an algorithm measure?
options: How the number of lines of code grows as more features are added to the program
How long the algorithm takes to run on a computer that has a given amount of memory
How the extra memory the algorithm uses grows with the size of its input
The size of the compiled program stored on disk after the code has been translated
explanation: Space complexity describes how the memory an algorithm needs, beyond the input itself, grows as the input grows. Lines of code, running time and the size of a compiled file are different measurements that do not describe memory use during execution.

title: Comparing growth rates
question: Which of these complexities grows fastest as n becomes very large?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
explanation: Exponential growth such as O(2^n) doubles with every extra item and soon overtakes any polynomial. Among the others, O(n^2) grows faster than O(n log n), which in turn grows faster than O(n).
